A study by Minassian et al. demonstrated that vaccination with RH5 significantly reduced the growth of malaria parasites in the blood stage and identified immune responses associated with this reduction. 2. Draper et al. reviewed recent advancements in recombinant protein-based malaria vaccines, highlighting their potential in combating malaria. 3. The development of adjuvants for vaccines, as well as for autoimmune and allergic diseases, was discussed in a report from Washington, D.C., emphasizing the role of small business innovation in advancing these technologies. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2014 on the quality, safety, and efficacy of recombinant malaria vaccines targeting both pre-erythrocytic and blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum. 5. WHO outlined preferred product characteristics for malaria vaccines in 2014, providing a framework for vaccine development and evaluation. 6. A WHO position paper from March 2022 summarized the organization's stance on malaria vaccines, including their role in public health strategies. 7. Tinto et al. conducted a three-year extension study on the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine, showing its long-term impact on severe malaria incidence in African children and infants. 8. Milligan and Moore presented statistical findings from the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine pilot evaluation, conducted 24 months after its introduction. 9. Penny et al. used phase III data and simulation models to predict the public health impact of the RTS,S malaria vaccine in malaria-endemic African countries. 10. Vekemans et al. pooled safety data from pediatric phase II trials of the RTS,S/AS malaria vaccine, providing insights into its safety profile. 11. Asante et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine when administered alongside routine immunization vaccines, with a 19-month follow-up. 12. Agnandji et al. assessed the safety and immunogenicity of the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine integrated into routine immunization programs. 13. Talaat et al. investigated the safety and immunogenicity of the Pfs25-EPA/Alhydrogel® transmission-blocking malaria vaccine in malaria-naïve adults. 14. Guimarães et al. explored the relationship between vaccines, adjuvants, and autoimmunity, discussing potential implications for vaccine development. 15. WHO published an operations manual in 2009 for managing malaria cases, providing practical guidance for healthcare providers. 16. WHO released a chart booklet in 2008 for managing childhood illnesses in high HIV settings, integrating malaria management strategies. 17. A 2011 WHO manual emphasized universal access to malaria diagnostic testing, outlining operational strategies for implementation. 18. A 1988 WHO memorandum discussed advancements in malaria diagnosis, including microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests. 19. WHO's 2016 manual on malaria microscopy quality assurance provided guidelines for ensuring diagnostic accuracy. 20. Kawamoto and Billingsley introduced fluorescence microscopy as a rapid diagnostic tool for malaria in a 1992 study. 21. WHO's 2003 publication on malaria diagnosis offered new perspectives on diagnostic methods and their applications. 22. A 2003 WHO meeting report addressed the challenges of implementing rapid diagnostic tests for malaria in endemic regions. 23. WHO's 2004 report discussed the use of rapid diagnostic tests for malaria, emphasizing their role in improving case management. 24. WHO's 2009 guidelines focused on the transportation, storage, and handling of malaria rapid diagnostic tests in healthcare settings. 25. WHO's 2018 report on malaria rapid diagnostic test performance summarized the results of product testing in round 8. 26. WHO's 2017 publication addressed the implications of false-negative rapid diagnostic test results due to Plasmodium falciparum HRP2/3 gene deletions. 27. Abba et al. reviewed the effectiveness of rapid diagnostic tests for diagnosing uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in endemic countries. 28. Thiam et al. reported a significant reduction in antimalarial drug consumption in Senegal following the nationwide introduction of rapid diagnostic tests. 29. Voller discussed the immunodiagnosis of malaria in a chapter from the book Malaria: Principles and Practice of Malariology. 30. Bates et al. highlighted the challenges of monitoring the impact of malaria interventions using diagnostic tools in a 2003 publication. 31. WHO's 2012 meeting report reviewed malaria diagnosis in low-transmission settings, providing evidence-based recommendations. 32. WHO's 2010 publication outlined best practices for procuring artemisinin-based antimalarial medicines. 33. Sinclair et al. reviewed the efficacy of artemisinin-based combination therapy for treating uncomplicated malaria in a 2009 Cochrane review. 34. Zani et al. evaluated the use of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a 2014 Cochrane review. 35. Tarning et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of piperaquine in children with uncomplicated malaria. 36. Tona Lutete et al. assessed the safety and effectiveness of pyronaridine-artesunate in real-world settings across five African countries. 37. Pryce et al. reviewed the efficacy of pyronaridine-artesunate for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a 2022 Cochrane review. 38. A 2013 pooled analysis examined the impact of dosing regimens on the antimalarial efficacy of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine. 39. Graves et al. reviewed the use of primaquine and other 8-aminoquinolines for reducing Plasmodium falciparum transmission. 40. White et al. provided a rationale for recommending a lower dose of primaquine as a gametocytocide in populations with high G6PD deficiency prevalence. 41. Recht et al. reviewed the safety of 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial medicines in a 2014 WHO publication. 42. WHO's 2015 policy brief recommended single-dose primaquine as a gametocytocide for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. 43. Desai et al. reviewed the epidemiology and burden of malaria during pregnancy, emphasizing its impact on maternal and neonatal health. 44. Accrombessi et al. investigated the effects of malaria during the first trimester of pregnancy on maternal and birth outcomes in Benin. 45. Walker et al. estimated the risk of placental infection and low birth weight attributable to Plasmodium falciparum malaria in Africa in 2010. 46. A 1979 study on Qinghaosu (artemisinin) highlighted its antimalarial properties and potential for clinical use. 47. White et al. explored the developmental toxicity of artesunate in animal models, linking embryonic erythroblast depletion to embryolethality. 48. Saito et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of artemisinin-based and quinine-based treatments for malaria during pregnancy. 49. Burger et al. compared artemisinin-based combination therapy with quinine for treating malaria in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. 50. Clark et al. studied the developmental toxicity and toxicokinetics of artesunate in monkeys, providing insights into its safety profile. This list provides detailed insights into the studies and guidelines related to malaria diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.
